Data Challenge - Resume Analyzer¶

Anna Kadurina

👋 Introduction¶

This project focuses on developing a Resume Analyzer – an intelligent tool that leverages natural language processing (NLP) to analyze resumes, extract structured information, and provide feedback using deep learning models. The long-term vision is to create a career assistant that helps job seekers craft effective resumes by simulating how AI-driven Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) might evaluate them. This notebook represents the first phase of the development: preparing the data and training a model for Named Entity Recognition (NER) and resume scoring.

1. 🌍 Domain Understanding¶

In today’s competitive job market, resumes play a critical role in making a strong first impression. Many organizations use automated systems to screen resumes, and poor formatting, lack of keywords, or missing sections often result in qualified candidates being filtered out prematurely.

This project addresses that issue by using AI to replicate the resume evaluation process. The system will identify key information such as skills, education, and job experience from unstructured text and provide suggestions for improvement. The immediate goal is to train a model capable of extracting relevant resume entities and scoring them using rule-based logic.

2. 📦 Data Provisioning¶

Data Requirements¶

Data Elements¶

🧾 Textual Data¶
Resume Content¶
  • Data Type: Free-form Text
  • Example: Full resume content including education, skills, and work experience.
  • Purpose: Source for Named Entity Recognition (NER) and scoring.
  • Content: Unstructured, semi-formatted text.
Named Entities (NER Output)¶
  • Data Type: Token Spans with Labels
  • Example:
    • Python → Skill
    • Harvard University → College Name
    • Software Engineer → Designation
  • Purpose: Structured extraction from resume text.
  • Format: BIO-tagging (Begin, Inside, Outside)
📊 Categorical Data¶
Resume Category (Optional)¶
  • Data Type: Category Label
  • Example: Data Science, HR, Web Developer
  • Purpose: Used for testing generalizability or future classification
  • Source: Gaurav Dutta Dataset
💬 Synthetic Data (Generated with ChatGPT)¶
Artificially Created Resumes¶
  • Data Type: Textual (same structure as real resumes)
  • Example: A ChatGPT-generated resume for a Marketing Manager with 10 years of experience
  • Purpose: Supplement real data to increase diversity across roles, styles, and backgrounds

Data Volume¶

To train robust NLP models, a significant amount of labeled and unlabeled text data is needed. For this project:

  • A minimum of 1000 labeled resumes is preferred for effective NER training.
  • Unlabeled resumes will support testing and rule-based scoring logic.
  • Synthetic resumes generated using ChatGPT will supplement the datasets to increase diversity and realism.

Data Variety¶

The model should generalize well across industries and job roles. Therefore, the data must include:

  • Resumes from various domains: tech, HR, education, healthcare, etc.
  • Different writing styles: concise bullet points, paragraph-style narratives.
  • Varying levels of experience: entry-level to executive.

Data Quality Standards¶

High-quality training data must be:

  • Correctly annotated: Entities like skills and education must be accurately labeled.
  • Consistent: Annotation format must follow BIO tagging conventions.
  • Readable and clean: No corrupted or unreadable files.

🗂️ Data Collection¶

Data Sources¶

Primary Datasets:

  • DataTurks Resume NER: JSON-based dataset with annotated resume entities.
  • Gaurav Dutta Resume Dataset: A collection of text-based resumes categorized by job roles.

Supplementary Data:

  • Synthetic Resumes: Created using ChatGPT prompts tailored for industry, seniority level, and writing style diversity. These will fill gaps in underrepresented domains and enhance model robustness.

Collecting the data¶

  • The datasets will be downloaded from Kaggle and stored locally in raw format.
  • Synthetic data will be generated using guided prompts and stored alongside the real datasets.
  • A preprocessing pipeline will convert the datasets into a format compatible with Hugging Face Transformers, using BIO-tagging for labeled text.

Data Storage¶

For the duration of development:

  • All files will be stored in a local project folder with the following structure:

⚖️ Ethical Considerations¶

As this project involves analyzing resume content—potentially containing sensitive personal data—ethical awareness is essential throughout the data lifecycle. Below are the key ethical dimensions and how they are addressed in this project.

1. Data Privacy¶

Resumes frequently include personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, and employer names. Exposure or misuse of such data could compromise user privacy.

Mitigation Measures:

  • Anonymization: All PII will be removed or obfuscated before using any data for training or evaluation.
  • No Storage of User Data: During prototype testing, any resumes submitted by users will be processed temporarily and never stored.
  • Local Processing: Data remains in a local environment; no resumes are uploaded to public clouds or external APIs.

2. Bias and Fairness¶

AI models trained on biased datasets can amplify societal inequities, especially in hiring. For example, they may favor certain degrees, schools, or professional titles based on historical data.

Mitigation Measures:

  • Synthetic Diversity: Artificial resumes created with ChatGPT will include varied names, backgrounds, job roles, and education types.
  • Bias Testing: The model will be tested on resumes representing diverse genders, regions, and industries to observe output consistency.
  • Score Explanation: Scoring logic will be transparent and rules-based to avoid learned bias in feedback.

3. Transparency and Explainability¶

Users must understand why they received a certain score or suggestion.

Practices for Transparency:

  • All feedback is based on clearly extractable entities (e.g., missing skills, lack of education info).
  • The system avoids black-box scoring. For example:
    "Your resume is missing a skills section" is more helpful than "Score: 4".

4. Misuse Prevention¶

An AI-based resume evaluator could be misused to unfairly filter candidates in automated hiring tools.

Boundaries of Use:

  • This tool is designed for self-assessment and guidance, not as a gatekeeping mechanism.
  • Clear disclaimers will inform users that the feedback is meant to assist—not replace—human judgment or professional resume reviews.

📊 Data Understanding¶

In this section, we analyze the structure, quality, and statistical properties of the DataTurks Resume NER dataset. This deep understanding ensures our data is reliable for fine-tuning a Named Entity Recognition (NER) model.

As we saw already, the dataset is stored in JSON lines format, where each record contains:

  • content: Full resume text
  • annotation: A list of entities, each with:
    • label: Entity type (e.g., "Skills")
    • points: Span with start, end, and text

Some of the resume labels don’t line up with the text, so we automatically search for them in the resume and fix their position. If found, we keep them. If not, we just note that the model couldn’t find them. To be able to do proper Data Understanding, we are going to to fix these potentially broken span annotations by finding the actual position (start, end) of each labeled entity (text) within the resume content. If the position is found using a regex match, the annotation is marked as fixed=True. Otherwise, it is flagged as unfixed for potential review.

In [3]:
def clean_and_fix_annotations(row):
    content = row["content"]
    fixed = []

    for ann in row["annotation"]:
        if not isinstance(ann.get("label"), list) or not ann.get("label"):
            continue
        if not isinstance(ann.get("points"), list) or not ann.get("points"):
            continue

        label = ann["label"][0]
        point = ann["points"][0]
        entity_text = point.get("text", "").strip()

        if not entity_text:
            continue

        matches = [m for m in re.finditer(re.escape(entity_text), content)]
        if matches:
            match = matches[0] 
            fixed.append({
                "label": label,
                "text": entity_text,
                "start": match.start(),
                "end": match.end(),
                "fixed": True
            })
        else:
            fixed.append({
                "label": label,
                "text": entity_text,
                "start": None,
                "end": None,
                "fixed": False
            })

    return fixed

df["clean_annotations"] = df.apply(clean_and_fix_annotations, axis=1)

total_entities = sum(len(anns) for anns in df["clean_annotations"])
fixed_entities = sum(1 for anns in df["clean_annotations"] for ann in anns if ann["fixed"])

🛠️ Data Preparation¶

In this section, we transform the cleaned dataset into a format suitable for fine-tuning a transformer-based Named Entity Recognition (NER) model. This involves converting annotated text spans into token-level BIO labels, tokenizing the resume text using a Hugging Face tokenizer, and optionally enriching the dataset with synthetic examples.

1. Synthetic Resume Generation¶

To improve the diversity and generalizability of the model, we enrich the training data with synthetic resumes. These are generated using ChatGPT prompts and are meant to fill gaps in underrepresented industries or experience levels.

Why Synthetic Data?¶

  • Boosts data volume for low-frequency entities
  • Adds domain variation (e.g., art, medicine, blue-collar jobs)
  • Reduces overfitting on a small dataset
In [ ]:
import time
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key="secret")

In the next code cells, we generate a large synthetic dataset of resumes using OpenAI's GPT-3.5 model. We define a list of 80 job titles and create a prompt template that requests a realistic, ATS-friendly resume for each role. For each job title, we generate 10 unique resumes by querying the OpenAI API, storing the output text along with an empty clean_annotations field (which will be used later for entity labeling). These resumes are saved to a local JSON file for reuse. After generation, we load the synthetic resumes into a DataFrame and merge them with our original annotated dataset, resulting in a combined dataset of over 1000 resumes. This expanded dataset will support better model training by increasing label diversity and helping the model generalize across job roles.

def generate_resume_prompt(job_title):
    return f"""Write a detailed and realistic resume for a person applying for the role of a {job_title}.
Include the following sections in plain text (no formatting): 
- Name
- Email address
- Phone number
- Location
- Summary
- Skills
- Education
- Work experience (with job title, company, and responsibilities)

Make it natural and ATS-friendly. Output as a single block of text.
"""
In [ ]:
synthetic_resumes = []
save_path = "data/synthetic_resumes.json"

for title in job_titles:
    for i in range(10):
        prompt = generate_resume_prompt(title)
        try:
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
                messages=[
                    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful resume writer."},
                    {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
                ],
                temperature=0.7,
                max_tokens=700
            )

            resume_text = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

            synthetic_resumes.append({
                "content": resume_text,

The next blocks of code focus on automatically annotating the synthetic resumes and aligning the entity spans. We start by defining the auto_annotate_resume function, which uses regular expressions to extract basic resume entities such as name, email address, phone number, location, and skills directly from the raw text. These annotations are applied to all synthetic resumes and stored in a new annotation column. We then merge the original and synthetic data into a unified DataFrame and use the clean_and_fix_annotations function to refine the annotations by locating exact character spans of each entity in the content. This prepares the data for model training by generating standardized and reliable clean_annotations for every resume.

In [4]:
def auto_annotate_resume(content):
    annotations = []

    first_line = content.strip().split("\n")[0].strip()
    if len(first_line.split()) <= 4:
        match = re.search(re.escape(first_line), content)
        if match:
            annotations.append({
                "label": ["Name"],
                "points": [{"text": first_line, "start": match.start(), "end": match.end()}]
            })

    email_match = re.search(r"\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}\b", content)
    if email_match:
        annotations.append({
            "label": ["Email Address"],
            "points": [{"text": email_match.group(), "start": email_match.start(), "end": email_match.end()}]
        })

    location_match = re.search(r"\b(?:[A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s[A-Z][a-z]+)?)\s*,\s*[A-Z]{2,}\b", content)
    if location_match:
        annotations.append({
            "label": ["Location"],
            "points": [{"text": location_match.group(), "start": location_match.start(), "end": location_match.end()}]
        })

    phone_match = re.search(r"(\+?\d{1,3})?[\s-]?\(?\d{2,4}\)?[\s.-]?\d{3,4}[\s.-]?\d{4}", content)
    if phone_match:
        annotations.append({
            "label": ["Phone Number"],
            "points": [{"text": phone_match.group(), "start": phone_match.start(), "end": phone_match.end()}]
        })

    skills_match = re.search(r"(?i)(skills|technical skills)\s*[:\-]?\s*(.+)", content)
    if skills_match:
        skills_text = skills_match.group(2).split("\n")[0].strip()
        if skills_text:
            match = re.search(re.escape(skills_text), content)
            if match:
                annotations.append({
                    "label": ["Skills"],
                    "points": [{"text": skills_text, "start": match.start(), "end": match.end()}]
                })

    return annotations

def clean_and_fix_annotations(row):
    content = row["content"]
    fixed = []

    for ann in row["annotation"]:
        if not isinstance(ann.get("label"), list) or not ann.get("label"):
            continue
        if not isinstance(ann.get("points"), list) or not ann.get("points"):
            continue

        label = ann["label"][0]
        point = ann["points"][0]
        entity_text = point.get("text", "").strip()

        if not entity_text:
            continue

        matches = [m for m in re.finditer(re.escape(entity_text), content)]
        if matches:
            match = matches[0] 
            fixed.append({
                "label": label,
                "text": entity_text,
                "start": match.start(),
                "end": match.end(),
                "fixed": True
            })
        else:
            fixed.append({
                "label": label,
                "text": entity_text,
                "start": None,
                "end": None,
                "fixed": False
            })

    return fixed

df_combined["clean_annotations"] = df_combined.apply(clean_and_fix_annotations, axis=1)

2. Entity Balancing¶

Next, we clean the resume annotations by filtering out any entities that are not part of a predefined valid set. We use the filter_valid_annotations function to keep only those entities that are both marked as fixed and belong to the expected categories (like name, skills, designation, etc.). We then isolate the resumes that contain at least one valid annotation and store them in df_ready, ensuring we only train our model on meaningful data. A random sample is printed for inspection, followed by a bar plot that visualizes the frequency distribution of each entity label. This gives us an overview of the balance and coverage of the labeled data before training.

In [9]:
valid_entities = {
    "NAME", "EMAIL_ADDRESS", "LOCATION", "SKILLS", "DESIGNATION",
    "COMPANIES_WORKED_AT", "DEGREE", "COLLEGE_NAME", "GRADUATION_YEAR"
}

def filter_valid_annotations(annotations):
    return [
        ann for ann in annotations
        if ann.get("fixed") and ann["label"].upper().replace(" ", "_") in valid_entities
    ]

df_combined["clean_annotations"] = df_combined["clean_annotations"].apply(filter_valid_annotations)

3. Job Tittles Cleaning¶

The next step focuses on cleaning and analyzing the job titles extracted from the resumes. Since raw titles often contain inconsistent formatting, abbreviations (like "Sr."), and irrelevant or noisy text, we define the clean_job_title function to standardize them. This includes expanding abbreviations, removing unwanted characters, and filtering out generic or uninformative titles like “intern” or “trainee.”

In [11]:
def clean_job_title(raw_title):
    title = raw_title.lower().strip()

    replacements = {
        r"\bsr\.?\b": "senior",
        r"\bjr\.?\b": "junior",
        r"\bmgr\b": "manager",
        r"\bdev\b": "developer",
        r"\bassoc\.?\b": "associate",
        r"\bit\b": "it",
        r"\bqa\b": "quality assurance",
        r"\bdba\b": "database administrator"
    }
    for pattern, replacement in replacements.items():
        title = re.sub(pattern, replacement, title)

    noise_keywords = [
        "student", "intern", "trainee", "contestant", "fresher", "job",
        "training", "content analyst", "arabic language", "2001"
    ]
    if any(noise in title for noise in noise_keywords):
        return None

    title = re.sub(r"[^a-z\s]", "", title)
    title = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", title).strip()

    if len(title) < 3:
        return None

    return title

3. 🔮 Predictions¶

In this chapter we are going to build our models, train and evaluate them.

Preprocessing - BERT¶

To prepare the resume data for Named Entity Recognition (NER) model training, we first tokenize the text and align entity annotations to individual tokens. We use the BERT tokenizer (bert-base-cased) from Hugging Face Transformers to convert resume text into input IDs suitable for the model. Since annotations can vary in structure, we ensure they're consistently formatted using a helper function that flattens any nested annotation lists. We then extract all unique entity labels (e.g., EMAIL_ADDRESS, SKILLS, etc.) and apply the standard BIO tagging scheme (Begin, Inside, Outside) to capture multi-token entities effectively. Each token is assigned a corresponding label ID, with padding tokens ignored during training (-100).

To improve performance and avoid memory issues, the dataset is processed in batches, and once tokenized, it is saved to disk. In this step, we load that saved dataset using load_from_disk, allowing us to resume work efficiently without reprocessing. This results in a clean, structured dataset that can be directly fed into a transformer model for training.

In [ ]:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from datasets import Dataset

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")

def fix_nested_annotations(anns):
    if isinstance(anns, list) and len(anns) > 0 and isinstance(anns[0], list):
        anns = [item for sublist in anns for item in sublist]
    return anns

df_combined["clean_annotations"] = df_combined["clean_annotations"].apply(fix_nested_annotations)

unique_labels = sorted({
    ent["label"].upper().replace(" ", "_")
    for anns in df_combined["clean_annotations"]
    for ent in anns if isinstance(ent, dict) and ent.get("fixed", False)
})

label_list = ["O"] + [f"B-{l}" for l in unique_labels] + [f"I-{l}" for l in unique_labels]
label2id = {label: idx for idx, label in enumerate(label_list)}
id2label = {idx: label for label, idx in label2id.items()}
In [ ]:
def preprocess(batch):
    tokenized_batch = tokenizer(
        batch["content"],
        padding="max_length",
        truncation=True,
        max_length=512,
        return_offsets_mapping=True
    )

    all_labels = []

    for i in range(len(batch["content"])):
        labels = ["O"] * len(tokenized_batch["input_ids"][i])
        annotations = batch["clean_annotations"][i]

        for ent in annotations:
            if not isinstance(ent, dict) or not ent.get("fixed", False):
                continue
            ent_start, ent_end = ent["start"], ent["end"]
            ent_label = ent["label"].upper().replace(" ", "_")

            for j, (start, end) in enumerate(tokenized_batch["offset_mapping"][i]):
                if start is None or end is None or tokenized_batch["attention_mask"][i][j] == 0:
                    continue
                if start >= ent_start and end <= ent_end:
                    labels[j] = f"B-{ent_label}" if start == ent_start else f"I-{ent_label}"

        label_ids = [label2id.get(tag, 0) for tag in labels]
        label_ids = [
            label_id if tokenized_batch["attention_mask"][i][j] == 1 else -100
            for j, label_id in enumerate(label_ids)
        ]
        all_labels.append(label_ids)

    tokenized_batch["labels"] = all_labels
    tokenized_batch.pop("offset_mapping")
    return tokenized_batch

Modelling - BERT¶

We load a pre-trained BERT model for token classification using bert-base-cased as the backbone. This model is specifically designed for sequence labeling tasks such as Named Entity Recognition (NER). By providing the num_labels, id2label, and label2id mappings, we customize the model for our resume-specific entity labels.

This step equips the model with the architecture needed to classify each token into one of our defined entity categories (e.g., B-NAME, I-SKILLS, etc.), while leveraging the contextual understanding BERT has already learned from general English corpora.

In [ ]:
import gc
import torch

# to help with memory
gc.collect()
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
In [ ]:
model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(
    "bert-base-cased", 
    num_labels=len(label_list),
    id2label=id2label,
    label2id=label2id
)

Before training, we set up a DataCollatorForTokenClassification to ensure each input batch is padded correctly to a maximum length of 512 tokens. This step is essential for uniformity across batches and efficient GPU utilization. We also define a custom compute_metrics function using sklearn’s classification_report. It converts model predictions and true labels into their corresponding entity names, filtering out padding tokens (represented by -100). This allows us to evaluate performance using precision, recall, and F1-score for each entity type.

Next, we configure the training process with TrainingArguments, specifying:

  • 6 training epochs
  • batch size of 8 for both training and evaluation
  • weight decay for regularization
  • logging and evaluation at the end of each epoch

Finally, we create a Trainer instance from Hugging Face's transformers library, passing the model, datasets, tokenizer, data collator, and metric function.

In [28]:
data_collator = DataCollatorForTokenClassification(
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    padding="max_length",
    max_length=512,
    return_tensors="pt"
)

def compute_metrics(pred):
    predictions, labels = pred
    predictions = predictions.argmax(axis=-1)

    true_labels, true_preds = [], []

    for p, l in zip(predictions, labels):
        current_true = []
        current_pred = []
        for pred_label, true_label in zip(p, l):
            if true_label != -100:
                current_true.append(id2label[true_label])
                current_pred.append(id2label[pred_label])
        true_labels.append(current_true)
        true_preds.append(current_pred)

    return classification_report(true_labels, true_preds, output_dict=True)

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./results",
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    per_device_train_batch_size=8,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=8,
    num_train_epochs=6,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_dir="./logs",
    logging_steps=10
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=tokenized_dataset["train"],
    eval_dataset=tokenized_dataset["test"],
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    data_collator=data_collator, 
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics
)

We will be plotting now the training and validation loss over the 6 epochs. The training loss decreased sharply and stabilized below 0.05, indicating that the model learned effectively from the expanded dataset. Validation loss also dropped early and stabilized around 0.08, showing good generalization without significant overfitting. This is a strong indicator that the model is learning to extract entities accurately and consistently.

The evaluation results of the BERT model trained on 1000 resumes demonstrate a substantial improvement in performance compared to the earlier 220-resume model. Core entities such as NAME, EMAIL_ADDRESS, and LOCATION achieved exceptionally high F1-scores (up to 1.00 for NAME), indicating near-perfect recognition. More importantly, entities that previously performed poorly due to limited training examples—such as SKILLS, YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE, and GRADUATION_YEA - now show significant gains, reaching F1-scores of 0.66, 0.71, and 0.72 respectively. Common resume fields like COMPANIES_WORKED_AT and DESIGNATION also perform robustly, with F1-scores above 0.90. Overall, the macro average F1-score improved from approximately 0.42 to 0.82, demonstrating that the model now handles both frequent and rare labels much more effectively. This confirms the value of expanding the dataset with synthetic and annotated resumes, making the model a much stronger candidate for real-world resume parsing tasks.

The confusion matrix illustrates strong overall performance, with most predictions correctly aligned along the diagonal. High-accuracy categories such as B-NAME, I-NAME, B-EMAIL_ADDRESS, and I-EMAIL_ADDRESS show minimal misclassification, confirming the model's reliability for core resume fields. Importantly, more challenging entities like I-SKILLS, I-GRADUATION_YEAR, and I-COLLEGE_NAME also show concentrated predictions in their correct columns, though with occasional confusion with similar entities. This reflects improved but still imperfect boundary detection, especially for multi-token fields. Overall, the matrix confirms consistent and accurate label classification across most entity types.

Comparison to 220-Resume Model¶

Metric 220 Resumes 1000 Resumes
Final training loss ~0.16 ~0.02
Validation loss ~0.29 ~0.08
Macro F1-score ~0.42 ~0.82
Entity recognition Only common labels (e.g. NAME, EMAIL) had good performance More labels like SKILLS, GRADUATION_YEAR, YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE improved
Overfitting signs Minor overfitting, validation loss plateaued early Minimal overfitting, stable training and evaluation loss curves
Training stability Noisy loss curve with slow convergence Smooth convergence and consistent evaluation across epochs

Increasing the data to 1000 resumes led to better convergence, lower losses, and improved generalization. The model now performs better not only on frequent entities but also on rarer ones that were previously neglected due to data sparsity. The training curve shows no sign of overfitting, which means even more data could help, or the model could be made more complex (e.g. RoBERTa).

Preprocessing - RoBERTa¶

After achieving strong results with BERT on 1000 resumes, we continue by training and evaluating a RoBERTa-based model to further explore performance improvements. RoBERTa is an optimized variant of BERT that removes the next sentence prediction objective and is trained with dynamic masking and more data, often resulting in better downstream performance. By applying RoBERTa to our named entity recognition task, we aim to assess whether its enhanced pretraining contributes to better generalization and entity extraction - especially on challenging fields like SKILLS or YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE. The comparison with BERT will help us validate if RoBERTa provides measurable gains in both precision and consistency.

To prepare the data for training with RoBERTa, we tokenize each resume using the roberta-base tokenizer while preserving the character-to-token alignment through offset_mapping. This allows us to accurately project entity span annotations (like names or skills) from the raw text onto the tokenized representation. For each token, we initialize a sequence of labels using the BIO format (B-, I-, O) to represent the beginning and continuation of named entities. The corresponding label indices are then mapped using label2id, with padding tokens masked by assigning -100 to ignore them during loss computation. This ensures the model is trained only on relevant tokens. Due to memory limitations, the preprocessing and splitting were run once, saved to disk, and reloaded for model training.

In [8]:

import torch

gc.collect()
torch.cuda.empty_cache()
In [9]:
def compute_metrics(pred):
    predictions, labels = pred
    predictions = predictions.argmax(axis=-1)

    true_labels, true_preds = [], []

    for p, l in zip(predictions, labels):
        current_true = []
        current_pred = []
        for pred_label, true_label in zip(p, l):
            if true_label != -100:
                current_true.append(id2label[true_label])
                current_pred.append(id2label[pred_label])
        true_labels.append(current_true)
        true_preds.append(current_pred)

    return classification_report(true_labels, true_preds, output_dict=True)
In [ ]:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

roberta_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roberta-base")

def preprocess_roberta(example):
    tokenized = roberta_tokenizer(
        example["content"],
        padding="max_length",
        truncation=True,
        max_length=512,
        return_offsets_mapping=True
    )

    labels = ["O"] * len(tokenized["input_ids"])

    for ent in example["clean_annotations"]:
        if not ent.get("fixed", False):
            continue
        ent_start, ent_end = ent["start"], ent["end"]
        ent_label = ent["label"].upper().replace(" ", "_")

        for i, (start, end) in enumerate(tokenized["offset_mapping"]):
            if start is None or end is None:
                continue
            if start >= ent_start and end <= ent_end:
                labels[i] = f"B-{ent_label}" if start == ent_start else f"I-{ent_label}"

    label_ids = [label2id.get(tag, 0) for tag in labels]
    label_ids = [
        label_id if tokenized["attention_mask"][i] == 1 else -100
        for i, label_id in enumerate(label_ids)
    ]

    tokenized["labels"] = label_ids
    tokenized.pop("offset_mapping")
    return tokenized

Modeling - RoBERTa¶

For the modeling phase, we use distilroberta-base, a lighter and faster variant of RoBERTa that retains over 95% of its language understanding capabilities while reducing model size and training time. We load both the tokenizer and model using Hugging Face Transformers. The model is configured for token classification by specifying the number of unique labels in our dataset and providing mappings between label indices and their string representations (id2label and label2id). This setup enables the model to predict a class label for each token in a resume, supporting fine-grained entity extraction with efficient resource usage.

In [ ]:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForTokenClassification
 
roberta_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("distilroberta-base")
 
roberta_model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(
    "distilroberta-base",
    num_labels=len(label_list),
    id2label=id2label,
    label2id=label2id
)

Some weights of RobertaForTokenClassification were not initialized from the model checkpoint at distilroberta-base and are newly initialized: ['classifier.bias', 'classifier.weight']
You should probably TRAIN this model on a down-stream task to be able to use it for predictions and inference.

We configure the training pipeline for RoBERTa using Hugging Face's Trainer API. First, we define a DataCollatorForTokenClassification to handle padding and batching of input sequences during training. Then, we specify TrainingArguments, such as the number of epochs (6), batch sizes, evaluation and checkpointing strategies, logging frequency, and output directories. The Trainer is initialized with the model, tokenizer, datasets, and the metric function for evaluation. We then launch training with .train() and save the fine-tuned model to a local directory.

In [14]:
from transformers import DataCollatorForTokenClassification, TrainingArguments, Trainer

roberta_data_collator = DataCollatorForTokenClassification(
    tokenizer=roberta_tokenizer,
    padding="max_length",
    max_length=512,
    return_tensors="pt"
)

roberta_training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./results_roberta",
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    per_device_train_batch_size=8,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=8,
    num_train_epochs=6,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_dir="./logs_roberta",
    logging_steps=10
)

roberta_trainer = Trainer(
    model=roberta_model,
    args=roberta_training_args,
    train_dataset=tokenized_roberta["train"],
    eval_dataset=tokenized_roberta["test"],
    tokenizer=roberta_tokenizer,
    data_collator=roberta_data_collator,
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics
)

roberta_trainer.train()

roberta_trainer.save_model("models/roberta_ner")

Now, we plot again the training and validation loss over epochs. Training loss decreases rapidly during the first two epochs and continues to drop steadily across all six epochs, eventually stabilizing around 0.02. Validation loss follows a similar pattern, converging around 0.04 and remaining stable thereafter, with no indication of overfitting. This suggests that the model is learning effectively and generalizing well to unseen data. Compared to the BERT model, RoBERTa achieves comparable, if not slightly better, training dynamics—especially in terms of convergence speed and final loss levels. The consistent gap between training and validation loss also indicates that regularization and hyperparameter settings are well-balanced.

The classification report for the RoBERTa model highlights a strong performance across nearly all entity types. High-frequency entities such as NAME, EMAIL_ADDRESS, and LOCATION continue to achieve near-perfect precision, recall, and F1-scores—demonstrating the model's ability to consistently recognize core resume information. Notably, RoBERTa performs better on more difficult entities compared to BERT: SKILLS now achieves an F1-score of 0.67 with an impressively high recall of 0.96, showing substantial improvement in identifying multi-token, semantically varied phrases. Likewise, GRADUATION_YEAR and YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE show balanced precision and recall, both scoring above 0.80 in F1. The macro average F1-score reaches 0.85, and the weighted average climbs to 0.92, confirming that RoBERTa generalizes well across both frequent and rare labels. This strong result validates RoBERTa’s effectiveness for NER in resume parsing tasks.

The confusion matrix for RoBERTa further confirms its strong entity recognition capabilities. Most predictions align closely with the diagonal, indicating high accuracy across entity classes. Especially for complex multi-token labels such as I-SKILLS, I-GRADUATION_YEAR, and I-YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE, the model shows a solid ability to correctly segment and classify span-level tokens. Very few misclassifications appear between adjacent labels—such as B-SKILLS vs I-SKILLS—which is expected in sequence tagging tasks. Overall, the matrix demonstrates that RoBERTa not only maintains consistency across high-frequency entities like NAME and EMAIL_ADDRESS, but also handles rarer entities with improved granularity and reduced noise compared to the earlier BERT results.

4. 📈 Resume Scoring Engine¶

In this section, we implement a Resume Scoring Engine that evaluates how well a candidate’s resume aligns with a specific job description. The final product is a web application where users can upload their resume and a description of a job posting, and receive structured insights in return. Our trained BERT or RoBERTa models extract key information from the resume in JSON format—such as skills, education, experience, etc.—and then a scoring function is used to assess how well the candidate fits the job. Afterwards, as an addition a feedback generated by an LLM is provided.

Initial Scoring Engine¶

This is the first version of the scoring engine with test data and a simple scoring algorithm where the CV is matched against the job discription and a score is provided.

In [3]:
# example json output from the BERT and RoBERTa
resume = {
    "skills": ["python", "nlp", "azure", "docker"],
    "degree": "MSc Computer Science",
    "years_of_experience": 3,
    "education_level": "bachelor"
}
In [4]:
# expample job posting that will be retrieved from the web app
job_posting = {
    "required_skills": ["python", "nlp", "mlflow", "azure"],
    "min_experience": 5,
    "preferred_degree": "bachelor"
}
In [ ]:
def score_resume(resume, job_posting):
    score = 0
    max_score = 100

    resume_skills = set(resume.get("skills", []))
    required_skills = set(job_posting.get("required_skills", []))
    matched_skills = resume_skills & required_skills
    skill_coverage = len(matched_skills) / len(required_skills) if required_skills else 0
    score += skill_coverage * 40

    extra_keywords = resume_skills - required_skills
    richness_ratio = len(extra_keywords) / 10 
    score += min(richness_ratio, 1.0) * 20

    degree = resume.get("education_level", "").lower()
    required = job_posting.get("preferred_degree", "").lower()
    if degree == required:
        score += 20
    elif degree in ["master", "phd"] and required == "bachelor":
        score += 15 
    elif degree == "bachelor" and required in ["master", "phd"]:
        score += 10 
    else:
        score += 0

    years = resume.get("years_of_experience", 0)
    required_years = job_posting.get("min_experience", 0)
    if years >= required_years:
        score += 20
    else:
        score += max(0, (years / required_years) * 20)

    return round(score, 2)

Advanced and Final Scoring Engine¶

Now, we continue with a more advanced scoring engine that is going to be actually used in the web app.

In the next code, we define score_resume_advanced_explained, a function that calculates a matching score between a candidate’s resume and a job posting, while also building a detailed explanation of how the score was computed. The function evaluates the resume on several key dimensions: skill coverage, preferred technologies, seniority level, education, and experience. Each of these contributes points toward a final score (capped at 100).

For each category, an explanation string is created that clearly shows how many points were awarded and why. This detailed feedback not only supports transparency but also helps users understand how their resume aligns with the job requirements.

In [ ]:
def score_resume_advanced_explained(resume, job_posting):
    score = 0
    explanation = {}

    def normalize_skill(s):
        return s.strip().lower()

    resume_skills = set(map(normalize_skill, resume.get("skills", [])))
    required_skills = set(map(normalize_skill, job_posting.get("required_skills", [])))
    preferred_tech = set(map(normalize_skill, job_posting.get("preferred_tech", [])))

    matched_skills = {r for r in required_skills for s in resume_skills if r in s or s in r}
    skill_coverage = len(matched_skills) / len(required_skills) if required_skills else 0
    skill_points = skill_coverage * 40
    score += skill_points
    explanation["Skill coverage"] = f"{len(matched_skills)}/{len(required_skills)} matched → +{round(skill_points,2)} points"

    tech_match = {p for p in preferred_tech for s in resume_skills if p in s or s in p}
    tech_coverage = len(tech_match) / len(preferred_tech) if preferred_tech else 0
    tech_points = tech_coverage * 10
    score += tech_points
    explanation["Preferred tech"] = f"{len(tech_match)}/{len(preferred_tech)} matched → +{round(tech_points,2)} points"

    resume_title = resume.get("designation", "").lower()
    summary = resume.get("summary", "").lower()
    seniority = job_posting.get("seniority_level", "").lower()
    seniority_points = 0
    if seniority in resume_title or seniority in summary:
        seniority_points = 10
    elif resume.get("years_of_experience", 0) >= job_posting.get("min_experience", 0) and seniority in ["senior", "lead"]:
        seniority_points = 5
    score += seniority_points
    explanation["Seniority level"] = f"Matched seniority: +{seniority_points} points"

    degree = resume.get("education_level", "").lower()
    required_degree = job_posting.get("preferred_degree", "").lower()
    edu_points = 0
    if "bachelor" in degree and "bachelor" in required_degree:
        edu_points = 20
    elif "master" in degree and required_degree == "bachelor":
        edu_points = 15
    elif "phd" in degree and required_degree == "bachelor":
        edu_points = 15
    elif "bachelor" in degree and required_degree in ["master", "phd"]:
        edu_points = 10
    elif degree == required_degree:
        edu_points = 20
    score += edu_points
    explanation["Education"] = f"{degree.title()} vs {required_degree.title()} → +{edu_points} points"

    years = resume.get("years_of_experience", 0)
    min_years = job_posting.get("min_experience", 0)
    exp_points = 0
    if years >= min_years:
        exp_points = 20
        exp_points += min(5, (years - min_years))
    else:
        exp_points = (years / min_years) * 20 if min_years else 0
    score += exp_points
    explanation["Experience"] = f"{years}/{min_years} years → +{round(exp_points,2)} points"

    final_score = round(min(score, 100), 2)
    return final_score, explanation

To improve the engine even more, we are going to use an LLM. We define the generate_resume_feedback function, which uses OpenAI’s GPT model (gpt-3.5-turbo) to provide personalized feedback on how a resume matches a given job description. The function constructs a detailed prompt that includes the extracted resume information (skills, designation, education, and experience) and the job posting details (required skills, preferred technologies, seniority level, degree, and minimum experience).

By sending this prompt to the language model, we ask it to compare the two and generate constructive feedback. Specifically, the AI highlights which skills are missing, which should be emphasized, and how the resume can be better tailored for the job. The result is a natural-language response that helps candidates understand how to strengthen their resume for a particular role.

In [ ]:
client = openai.OpenAI(api_key="secret")

def generate_resume_feedback(resume, job_posting):
    resume_text = f"""
    Resume Extracted:
    Skills: {', '.join(resume.get('skills', []))}
    Designation: {resume.get('designation', '')}
    Education: {resume.get('education_level', '')}
    Years of Experience: {resume.get('years_of_experience', '')}
    """

    job_text = f"""
    Job Description:
    Required Skills: {', '.join(job_posting.get('required_skills', []))}
    Preferred Tech: {', '.join(job_posting.get('preferred_tech', []))}
    Seniority Level: {job_posting.get('seniority_level', '')}
    Preferred Degree: {job_posting.get('preferred_degree', '')}
    Min Experience: {job_posting.get('min_experience', '')}
    """

    prompt = f"""
    Compare the following resume to the job description and provide feedback:
    - What skills are missing?
    - Which skills should be emphasized?
    - How could the resume be tailored better for this job?

    {resume_text}
    {job_text}
    """

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are an expert career coach."},
            {"role": "user", "content": prompt}
        ],
        temperature=0.7
    )

    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

In the next part, we load our fine-tuned RoBERTa model and tokenizer to extract key information from a resume text. The model performs Named Entity Recognition (NER) to identify entities like skills, degree, designation, and years of experience from the resume. After tokenizing the input resume, we run the model to predict entity labels for each token. We then iterate over the tokens and their predicted labels, reconstructing full entity texts where appropriate.

To improve robustness, we add a regex fallback: if certain entities (e.g., skills, degree, or experience) are missing from the model output, we use regular expressions to try to extract these details directly from the raw text. This hybrid approach ensures better coverage and reliability, even if the model fails to recognize some entities.

The final result is a structured dictionary, resume_extracted, which contains the extracted skills, degree, designation, and years of experience.

In [70]:
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("models/roberta_ner")
model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained("models/roberta_ner")
id2label = model.config.id2label

trainer = Trainer(model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer)

    "content": """Name: Emily Johnson

- Ensured cross-browser compatibility and responsive design

Feel free to contact me for further information or collaboration opportunities.

}

job_posting = {
    "required_skills": ["javascript", "react", "html", "css", "git"],
    "preferred_tech": ["angular", "cypress", "responsive design"],
    "seniority_level": "front-end developer",
    "preferred_degree": "bachelor",
    "min_experience": 3
}


inputs = tokenizer(
    test_resume_text["content"],
    return_tensors="pt",
    truncation=True,
    padding="max_length",
    max_length=512
)

outputs = model(**inputs)
predictions = outputs.logits.argmax(dim=-1)[0].tolist()
tokens = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(inputs["input_ids"][0])
labels = [id2label[p] for p in predictions]

resume_extracted = {
    "skills": [],
    "designation": "",
    "education_level": "",
    "years_of_experience": 0
}

current_entity = None
current_text = ""

for token, label in zip(tokens, labels):
    clean_token = token.replace("Ġ", "").replace("▁", "")
    
    if label == "O":
        if current_entity:
            if current_entity == "SKILLS":
                resume_extracted["skills"].append(current_text.strip())
            elif current_entity == "DEGREE":
                resume_extracted["education_level"] = current_text.strip()
            elif current_entity == "DESIGNATION":
                resume_extracted["designation"] = current_text.strip()
            elif current_entity == "YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE":
                try:
                    resume_extracted["years_of_experience"] = int(current_text.strip())
                except:
                    pass
            current_entity = None
            current_text = ""
    else:
        label_clean = label.split("-", 1)[-1]
        if current_entity == label_clean:
            current_text += " " + clean_token
        else:
            if current_entity:
                if current_entity == "SKILLS":
                    resume_extracted["skills"].append(current_text.strip())
                elif current_entity == "DEGREE":
                    resume_extracted["education_level"] = current_text.strip()
                elif current_entity == "DESIGNATION":
                    resume_extracted["designation"] = current_text.strip()
                elif current_entity == "YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE":
                    try:
                        resume_extracted["years_of_experience"] = int(current_text.strip())
                    except:
                        pass
            current_entity = label_clean
            current_text = clean_token

resume_extracted["skills"] = [s for s in resume_extracted["skills"] if s.strip()]
resume_extracted["designation"] = resume_extracted["designation"].strip()

content = test_resume_text["content"]

if not resume_extracted["skills"]:
    skills_match = re.search(r"Skills:\s*(.*?)(Education|Work Experience|$)", content, re.S | re.I)
    if skills_match:
        skills_section = skills_match.group(1)
        skills_list = re.findall(r"-\s*(.+)", skills_section)
        resume_extracted["skills"] = [s.strip() for s in skills_list]

if not resume_extracted["education_level"]:
    edu_match = re.search(r"Bachelor.*|Master.*|MSc.*|PhD.*", content, re.I)
    if edu_match:
        resume_extracted["education_level"] = edu_match.group().strip()

if resume_extracted["years_of_experience"] == 0:
    exp_match = re.search(r"(\d+)\s+years", content, re.I)
    if exp_match:
        resume_extracted["years_of_experience"] = int(exp_match.group(1))

print("\n📋 Extracted Resume Data (Hybrid):")
print(resume_extracted)

5. 🚀 Conclusion¶

At this stage of the project, we have successfully developed a robust and intelligent resume analysis system. Our journey began with data provisioning, where we generated ~800 high-quality synthetic resumes using OpenAI and combined them with a smaller annotated dataset from Kaggle. We implemented automatic annotation logic, followed by thorough cleaning and standardization to ensure data consistency.

We then built and trained two Named Entity Recognition (NER) models — BERT and RoBERTa — using HuggingFace Transformers. Our BERT model, trained on the expanded dataset of 1000 resumes, demonstrated significant improvements in macro F1-score over the initial 220-resume version. RoBERTa further complemented this with competitive performance, showing particular strength in extracting entities like SKILLS, GRADUATION_YEAR, and YEARS_OF_EXPERIENCE.

Building on these models, we designed an enhanced Resume Scoring Engine that evaluates resumes across multiple dimensions: skill match, preferred technologies, seniority level alignment, education fit, and years of experience. This engine not only generates a score normalized to a 100-point scale but also provides a detailed breakdown that transparently explains how the score was derived.

To enrich the user experience, we integrated a Large Language Model (LLM) (OpenAI’s GPT) to generate tailored, natural-language feedback. This feedback highlights missing or underemphasized skills, recommends improvements, and guides users on how to align their resumes more closely with a given job posting.

Finally, we wrapped this system in a user-friendly Streamlit web app, allowing users to upload or paste their resumes, enter job details, and instantly receive both structured resume extractions, a comprehensive fit score, and actionable AI-generated recommendations. The Streamlit app incorporates the logic provided in this notebook and can be found in the same zip file as this notebook.

Future Recommendations:

  • Continuously evaluate and fine-tune the NER models with additional real-world data to improve extraction accuracy.
